applicability: Any positive integer n, of any length. Write its decimal digits from the RIGHT as d0 (units), d1 (tens), d2 (hundreds), ...; form the alternating sum A(n) = d0 - d1 + d2 - d3 + ... Then n ≡ A(n) (mod 11), so n is divisible by 11 EXACTLY WHEN A(n) is a multiple of 11 — where 0, +11, -11, +22, ... all count as multiples. Direction matters for the value of A(n) (it must start at the units digit and alternate leftwards), but not for the yes/no verdict, since running it from the left only ever flips the sign of A(n). The 'exactly when' is asserted here only over the exhaustively checked finite domain 1 ≤ n ≤ 999999; see nulls[].
carry_case: 2915. The alternating sum is 5 - 1 + 9 - 2 = 11, which is NOT 0, yet 2915 = 11 × 265 is divisible by 11. So the tempting simplified form of the rule — 'the plus/minus digits must cancel to zero' — gives a false negative. The pass condition is 'A(n) is a multiple of 11', not 'A(n) = 0'. The same break appears with a negative total: 90728 gives 8 - 2 + 7 - 0 + 9 = 22, and 209 gives 9 - 0 + 2 = 11; both are divisible by 11 while failing the 'must be zero' form.

operand_draw.construction: test_subject = drawn_value = 3958; divisor = 11 (fixed by the method being taught).
operand_draw.construction_note: One integer drawn uniformly from [1000, 9999]. The range is a presentation choice declared before the draw: four digits is wide enough that trial division is genuinely annoying and narrow enough to fit the 500 px working line. The min_digits/max_digits/positive_only filter is redundant against that range (it rejected nothing, rate 0) and is purely rendering-driven — no filter here can express, and none was used to express, anything about divisibility. The draw produced 3958, which is NOT divisible by 11 (A = 9, and 3958 = 11 × 359 + 9). Per §3.4 the draw stands: a divisibility TEST has to answer 'no' as often as 'yes', so a negative verdict suits the method exactly. The alternating sum landing on 9 also lands the remainder for free, which is the strongest version of the payoff available from this draw.
operand_draw.carry_case_note: The carry case (2915) is deliberately constructed, not drawn: §3.4 governs the worked example's operands, while the caveat by definition must be a specific input that breaks the simplified rule. It is stated so the Verifier can test it directly.

candidates.verdict: different mechanism, same numeral. That lesson COMPUTES a product (split the digits, drop their sum between them, carry). This one TESTS an unknown number for a factor via an alternating digit sum, and returns a remainder. Neither procedure is derivable from the other by a viewer, and the inputs differ in kind (a chosen two-digit multiplicand vs any integer of any length). Not a paraphrase.

nulls.reason: The rule is claimed as an 'exactly when' for all positive integers, but core/verify/theorems.json whitelists no theorem about alternating digit sums modulo 11 (base-b-digit-sum-congruence covers digit sums mod b-1 = 9, not mod b+1 = 11). Per §3.2 an unproven universality claim is not accepted on assertion, so the claim is stated only over the exhaustive finite domain 1 ≤ n ≤ 999999, which the generator check enumerates in full. No claim is made outside that domain.
